pageSummary:
Carv.io – From time sheets to true capacity forecasting

Carv.io was born from a simple question most small and mid‑sized teams can't answer with their current tools: Are we staffed for the work that's really coming? Time trackers, ticket boards, and static resource calendars are good at recording the past and organizing the present, but they rarely help you see pipeline volatility, new skill demands, or the downstream impact of unexpected wins and delays. This case study outlines two working prototypes that push beyond record‑keeping toward simulation and prediction: a browser‑based pipeline simulator and a curved (Bezier) hours allocator.

The problem we set out to solve
SMEs need a planning approach that's fast to set up, cheap to run, and honest about uncertainty. They want to know whether today's people will cover tomorrow's work; how to cope with stressors like client slippage, internal hiring delays, or surprise sales; and where shortfalls or surpluses will emerge as projects enter, mature, or fall out of the pipeline. Existing tools don't model those dynamics—so we built ones that do.

Simulation framework v1.0 — modeling the pipeline
The simulation is a stand‑alone JavaScript app that runs entirely in the browser. It starts with a project template: up to five colored assignment blocks, each representing a role, arranged within a 26‑week window. Planners drag to reposition or resize blocks, capturing not just how much effort a role needs, but when it's needed. Every new deal that enters the pipeline clones this template, so patterns repeat consistently across many concurrent "project instances."

Capacity is explicit. For each active role, planners set full‑time equivalents (FTEs). The system converts FTEs to hours per week (1 FTE = 40 hours) and draws per‑role and total capacity lines. As FTE counts grow, the vertical scale expands automatically. A feed‑rate control governs how frequently new project instances appear from the right, so you can simulate slow trickles or rapid booking streaks.

Uncertainty is built in. Each project lives in one of four confidence zones—25%, 50%, 75%, 100%—based on where it sits along the sales‑to‑contract timeline. As time advances, projects cross boundaries; some progress, a proportion "dies off," and only the strongest reach 100%. Visual cues reinforce this: opacity tracks confidence (a 25% prospect renders at 25% opacity), and an optional ghost view compresses curves according to cumulative confidence, yielding a more realistic picture of probable workload rather than a best‑case pile‑up.

Results are live. The simulator continuously reports elapsed time, counts of past projects, totals in each confidence band, and role‑by‑role surplus/deficit against capacity. Because it's browser‑based, teams can explore scenarios quickly without standing up a backend.

Bezier allocation — shaping hours within a project
Capacity planning also hinges on how effort unfolds. Many tools assume flat distributions; real projects rarely behave that way. Our Bezier mini‑project lets planners shape a fixed budget of hours across a timeline using a quadratic Bezier curve driven by a single control point.

Drag the point to front‑load ramp‑up, peak midstream, or taper toward delivery—the system preserves total hours, pins start and end dates, and enforces sensible slopes (positive at the start, negative at the end) so curves remain realistic. A lightweight JSON model reads/writes the project's total budget, start/end week numbers, control‑point coordinates, and computed hours per week. Axes adjust on the fly: the horizontal scale labels "Week N" across year‑end rollovers; the vertical scale adapts to whatever weekly maximum the curve produces.

How it comes together
In practice, planners define a role pattern once, feed deals into the pipeline at a chosen rate, and watch as confidence‑weighted workloads rise and fall against declared capacity. When a particular project needs a non‑flat profile, they shape its curve with the Bezier editor—no spreadsheets, no manual re‑tabulation. The combination surfaces where and when pressure accumulates, which roles will be underwater, and what happens if sales velocity or kill‑rates change.

Why this is different

  • A systems‑theory lens. Instead of static calendars, Carv models flow—entry, attrition, maturation—and makes uncertainty visible.
  • Low‑resolution, high‑yield inputs. You can start with coarse budgets, durations, and FTE counts and only add detail when it materially improves decisions.
  • A foundation for recommendations. The simulator plus Bezier shaping provide scaffolding for a future engine that forecasts surpluses/shortfalls across multiple horizons.
  • Process‑agnostic by design. Whether your delivery resembles steps, waves, or something ad hoc, the framework can mirror it—and later ingest actuals from external time logs.
  • SME‑friendly. Running in the browser keeps cost and complexity low while still enabling meaningful scenario planning.

What's next
To move from prototype to product, we'll port the simulator into the Carv React app and back it with a Django/REST API for persistence and collaboration. Confidence modeling will get tunable kill‑rates, custom boundaries, and smarter arrival distributions. The Bezier editor will support multiple control points, editable start/end dates, and reusable curve templates (e.g., discovery‑heavy vs. implementation‑heavy). On top, we'll build a recommendation layer—statistical methods and ML informed by real time‑log data—to forecast staffing risk from one week out to six months. Finally, we'll invest in UX polish: richer visuals (heat maps, subtle animations), clearer ghost views, and mobile‑friendly interactions.

Outcome
These prototypes validate that a lightweight, simulation‑first approach can answer the staffing questions SMEs actually ask. By modeling the pipeline with confidence zones and letting planners sculpt per‑project effort realistically, Carv moves past retrospective tracking toward forward‑looking capacity management—the groundwork for a scalable, affordable portfolio planning system.
